introduction.text: The Argiletum was an ancient Roman street that ran from the Suburra district to the Roman Forum, serving as a commercial hub and later a passageway during the imperial age.

history.description: The Argiletum originally ran between the Comitium and the Basilica Pauli before being absorbed by the construction of the Imperial fora from the time of Julius Caesar onwards.
During the Flavian rule (AD 69–96), the Argiletum became a principal node of public space.
By the time of Martial (died about AD 103), the Argiletum had become a seedy district filled with taverns and brothels.
Varro claimed that the name of the street derived from a Greek scoundrel.
The first stretch of the Argiletum was replaced by the Forum of Nerva during the imperial age, but remained a passageway known as Forum Transitorium.
The Argiletum was known as the street of booksellers, mentioned by Horace, Martial, and Seneca.

design.description: The Argiletum branched into the Vicus Patricius (now Via Urbana) and the Clivus Suburanus (now Via in Selci) on its eastern side.
On its western side, the Argiletum ended between the Basilica Aemilia and the Curia.
During the imperial age, the first stretch of the Argiletum was replaced by the Forum of Nerva, which maintained a function of passageway and was also known as Forum Transitorium.

art.description: A quadrifrons (Tetrapylon) was located at the junction of the Roman Forum, the Argiletum, and the Forum of Caesar.
The Temple of Janus Geminus was located at the lower Argiletum.
